# The UCC domain, in one page

<!-- Generated by scripts/inject_domain_examples.py from docs/ucc-corpus.json and
     docs/domain-examples.json. Do not hand-edit; edit those and re-run. -->

The labs process commercial lien filings. You do not need to know the domain to do
them, but you do need to know what the fields mean — this page is the whole of it.
The course player carries the same material: the primer opens M00, and the glossary
sits in the nav drawer, reachable from every module.

---

## The Filing on Your Desk

Every module in this course processes the same kind of document, so it is worth ninety
seconds on what one actually is — the rest of the course assumes it.

A **UCC-1 financing statement** is a public record a lender files with a state Secretary of
State to announce a claim on a business's assets. Credit teams read these to answer one
question: _how much is already claimed against this company, and by whom?_ Here is one,
annotated:

**2024-FL-0012345 · UCC-1 · FLORIDA · ACTIVE**

- **Debtor** — ACME LOGISTICS & DISTRIBUTION, L.L.C.
  _← who owes. The company you are scoring._
- **Debtor address** — 1450 N.W. 107TH AVE, STE 310, MIAMI, FL 33172
  _← how you catch two shell names that are one operation._
- **Secured party** — FIRST CAPITAL EQUIPMENT FINANCE, INC.
  _← who lent, and now holds the claim._
- **Collateral** — ALL ACCOUNTS, INVENTORY, AND EQUIPMENT NOW OWNED OR HEREAFTER ACQUIRED, TOGETHER WITH ALL PROCEEDS THEREOF.
  _← what backs the loan. Free text, written by the filer — which is why it is also where injected instructions hide._
- **Filed** — 2024-03-11
- **Lapses** — 2029-03-11
  _← five years. A lapsed lien is not an active one._

That one is easy. The document that makes this a context engineering problem rather than a
parsing problem is its amendment:

**2024-FL-0024117 · UCC-3 · AMENDMENT**

- **Amends** — 2024-FL-0012345
- **Action** — Debtor name changed. See original filing.
- **Debtor** — **— not on this document —**
  _← the field you need. It is in the filing this one points at._

A **UCC-3** amends, continues or terminates an earlier filing, and it usually points at that
filing instead of restating it. Ask a model for the debtor name here and the name is simply
not in front of it. What happens next — a confident, correctly formatted, invented answer —
is the failure this entire course is about.

> Four more things worth knowing, all of them in the **UCC Glossary** in the nav drawer,
> reachable from every module: a name cut at 80 characters is the form's field width, not the
> company's legal name; `[REDACTED PER COURT ORDER]` means the correct answer is `null`; a
> termination means the debt is settled; and a filing takes days to weeks to become
> searchable, so a clean search means _no liens visible yet_, not _no liens_.

## The cast

The same companies recur across every module and lab, so a filing you meet in M20 is
one you already know.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Debtor** | ACME LOGISTICS & DISTRIBUTION, L.L.C. |
| **Secured party** | FIRST CAPITAL EQUIPMENT FINANCE, INC. |
| **Shared address** | 1450 N.W. 107TH AVE, STE 310, MIAMI, FL 33172 |

The shared address is the related-party signal: three unrelated-looking debtors file from it.

## The ten filings

Every filing id used in the course resolves to one of these. Each exists to teach one
specific failure.

| Filing | Type | Status | Edge case | What it is for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `2024-FL-0012345` | UCC-1 | active | clean | The baseline. Every field present, nothing ambiguous — the filing the pipeline handles correctly on day one. |
| `2024-FL-0012354` | UCC-1 | active | transposition-decoy | Deliberately one transposition away from ACME's filing, and a completely different debtor. It exists so two failures have teeth: an embedding model cannot separate the two ids (M09), and a summarisation step that rewrites 0012345 as 0012354 does not produce a broken reference — it silently points at someone else's lien (M18). |
| `2024-FL-0024117` | UCC-3 | active | amendment-pointer | The hard case, and the course's workhorse. The answer is NOT in this document — it is in the one this points at. A model asked to extract a debtor name from here will invent one unless the window carries the original. |
| `2024-FL-0019001` | UCC-1 | active | related-party | Same address as ACME, different name. The related-party signal only exists when both records are in the window at once — retrieval that returns the best-matching filing alone destroys it. |
| `2024-FL-0022100` | UCC-1 | active | related-party | The third filing from the shared address. Three debtors, one suite number, one overlapping secured party. |
| `2024-FL-0019988` | UCC-1 | active | corroborating | A second secured party against the same debtor, three months after the first. Used where two sources must agree: the state index and a credit bureau extract both name it, which is what makes it corroboration rather than a claim. |
| `2023-FL-0009880` | UCC-3 | terminated | termination | A closed lien. Counting it as active is the single most common lien-risk scoring error — status is a field, not an assumption. |
| `2024-TX-0004410` | UCC-1 | active | injection | Filing text is attacker-controlled free text. The collateral description is where an injection rides in — which is why filings enter the window fenced as data, never blended into instructions. |
| `2024-NY-0008812` | UCC-1 | active | redacted | There is no debtor name to extract. null is the correct answer, and a model that has only ever seen clean examples will not produce it. |
| `2024-CA-0031755` | UCC-1 | active | truncated | Exactly 80 characters, cut mid-word: INCORPORA is the tail of INCORPORATED. The field width, not the company, decided where this name ended. |

## Glossary

**UCC** — Uniform Commercial Code — the US state law governing secured lending.

> Article 9 covers security interests in business assets. When a lender wants public proof of
> its claim, it files a record with a state office.

**Lien** — A lender's registered claim on a business's assets.

> The thing every filing in this course records. The lien is the claim; the UCC-1 is the
> public document that announces it. Counting liens that have lapsed or been terminated is the
> fastest way to score a company wrong.

**Public record** — A filing anyone can search, with no permission needed.

> UCC filings are deliberately public — that is what puts other lenders on notice. It also
> means the text was written by the filer and not validated by the state.

**Debtor** — The business that owes.

> The entity whose assets are pledged. In lien-risk work this is the company you are scoring —
> getting its name exactly right is the whole extraction problem.

**Obligor** — Whoever is on the hook for the debt.

> Often the same entity as the debtor, but not always: related companies and guarantors can be
> obligors on one credit. Rolling several names into a single obligor is the point of
> related-party detection.

**Guarantor** — A third party who pays if the debtor does not.

> Frequently an owner signing personally, which ties a company's risk to an individual's.

**EIN** — Employer Identification Number — the IRS's id for a business.

> The one identifier that survives a name change, which is why matching on it beats matching
> on names. Most UCC filings do not carry one.

**Secured party** — The lender that holds the claim.

> Several secured parties filing against one debtor in a short window is itself a risk signal.

**Collateral** — What backs the loan.

> Free text, written by the filer. It ranges from one line to several pages, and it is where
> injected instructions hide.

**Blanket lien** — A lien over everything the business owns.

> Signalled by all-assets collateral language. It leaves nothing unencumbered for a later
> lender, so it moves a credit decision more than its dollar figure suggests.

**Proceeds** — Whatever the collateral turns into when it is sold.

> Standard collateral language extends the claim to the cash and receivables from selling the
> pledged goods, so the lien does not evaporate the moment inventory ships.

**After-acquired** — Assets the debtor buys later, covered by a lien signed today.

> The phrase 'now owned or hereafter acquired' pulls future property into an existing claim.
> It is what makes a blanket lien blanket.

**Financing statement** — The formal name for the filed record.

> A UCC-1 is a financing statement; the two get used interchangeably. It states who owes, who
> lent, and what backs the loan — nothing more.

**UCC-1** — The original financing statement — the lien itself.

> Carries the debtor, the secured party, the collateral and the filing date. Self-contained:
> everything you need is on the document.

**UCC-3** — An amendment, continuation or termination of an existing UCC-1.

> The hard case. A UCC-3 usually points at the filing it changes rather than restating it, so
> the field you want sits in a document that is not in front of you.

**Amendment** — A UCC-3 that changes an existing filing.

> Changes a name, an address or the collateral. It usually points at the original filing
> instead of restating it, which is why the field you need is often not on the document in
> front of you.

**Filing ID** — The record's public identifier, e.g. 2024-FL-0012345.

> Year, state, sequence. Tokenizers shred these into digit-by-digit pieces, which is why they
> cost far more tokens than their length suggests.

**Perfection** — Filing publicly so the claim beats later creditors.

> Filing is what makes the security interest enforceable against others. An unperfected
> interest is nearly worthless in a bankruptcy.

**Lapse** — A UCC-1 expires five years after filing unless continued.

> A lapsed lien is not an active one. Scoring on filing date without checking lapse inflates
> risk.

**Continuation** — A UCC-3 that extends a filing for another five years.

> Only valid in the six months before lapse — so its presence dates the underlying debt.

**Termination** — A UCC-3 that closes the lien.

> The debt is settled. Counting terminated filings as active is the most common lien-risk
> scoring error.

**Related party** — Distinct debtor names that are really one operation.

> Usually caught by a shared address, a shared officer, or an overlapping secured party — and
> only when both records sit in the window together.

**Truncation** — A debtor name cut off at the filing form's field width.

> Around 80 characters, names stop mid-word. The cut is an artifact of the form, not the
> company's legal name.

**Redaction** — A name withheld by court order.

> The document says [REDACTED PER COURT ORDER]. The correct extraction is null with a flag —
> not a guess, and not an error.

**Search-to-reflect lag** — The days between a filing being made and being searchable.

> Typically one to several weeks, varying by state. A clean search does not mean no liens; it
> means no liens visible yet.

**Secretary of State** — The state office where filings are made and searched.

> Each of the fifty runs its own index and its own search rules, so 'the record' depends on
> which state you asked.

**Filing office** — The state Secretary of State that holds the records.

> Each state formats, paginates and OCRs differently, so the same logical field arrives in
> fifty shapes.
